To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cardiovascular response to baroreceptor denervation differs depending on the location of the lesion and that 24-hour continuous recordings of mean blood pressure and heart rate are more accurate than 1-hour continuous recordings in estimating the altered cardiovascular activity in baroreceptor-denerved rats.

1-hour recordings of mean arterial blood pressure and heart rate are sufficient to assess the cardiovascular responses of baroreceptor-deanervated rats, and that the differences in cardiovascular responses between rats with central and peripheral denervation of their baroceptors are due to the more complete destruction of central neurons and circuits by central baroreceptor denervation.
the average mean arterial pressures of rats with central and peripheral baroceptor denervation are similar, and both groups have an increase in the lability of their mean arterial pressures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an animal model that will be useful in studying the role of the baroreceptor reflex in hypertension.
the role of baroreceptor reflexes in the regulation of blood pressure.
the effects of central and peripheral lesions of baroreceptor reflex pathways on the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate (HR) responses to changes in blood pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
1-hour and longer-term recordings of mean arterial pressures are equally useful for estimating the cardiovascular activity of baroceptor-denervated and sham-operated rats.
1-hour recordings are sufficient for the assessment of cardiovascular activity in conscious, unrestrained baroreceptor-denervation rats.
1-hour recordings of blood pressure are as good as 24-hour recordings in terms of detecting the effects of baroreceptor denervation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the nucleus tractus of the rat is an area of the brain that is important in regulating blood pressure and heart rate, and that the nucleus tract solitarii is the most important area of the brain in regulating the blood pressure of the rat.
the cardiovascular system of rats with nucleus solitarii or sinoaortic denervations is more sensitive to movement-related changes in blood pressure and heart rate.
the cardiovascular responses of baroreceptor denervated rats can be accurately assessed using short term recordings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
short-term continuous blood pressure recording in rats is sufficient for assessing baroreflex function and that this method can be easily implemented in a variety of research laboratories.
the 1-hour recordings are sufficient for the purpose of our study.
short-term continuous recording of blood pressure and heart rate is sufficient to detect the altered cardiovascular activity in rats that have undergone baroreceptor denervation.
